name: Nicholas Cabasilas
knownFor: A learned layman of the emperor's household and an envoy in the civil war, who wrote The Life in Christ and a commentary on the Divine Liturgy. He taught that the life in Christ is given through baptism, chrismation and the Eucharist, and can be lived at home and at work.
dates: The notice from Fabricius in Migne says he flourished about 1350. John Kantakouzenos names him as an envoy in 1346, as joining the emperor's plan to withdraw in 1349, and as still a layman in 1353. A synod's record of September 1350 lists him in the emperor's household. No witness gives his birth or death.
place: Thessalonica, which chose him as its envoy in 1346. Berroia, where he met Manuel Kantakouzenos. Constantinople, where he was of the emperor's household and was put forward for patriarch.
role: Layman of the imperial household; envoy; theologian of the sacraments

keyWorks.title: The Life in Christ
keyWorks.about: seven books on how baptism, chrismation and the Eucharist give, complete and keep the life in Christ. Jacob Pontanus put six books into Latin in 1604; Wilhelm Gass printed the Greek at Greifswald in 1849, and Migne prints Greek and Latin side by side.

keyWorks.title: Commentary on the Divine Liturgy
keyWorks.about: on how everything done in the Liturgy makes the faithful holy and shows the Savior's saving work. Gentian Hervet put it into Latin at Venice in 1548, and Fronto Ducaeus printed the Greek in 1624.

keyWorks.title: Sermon against usurers
keyWorks.about: against lending at interest. No labor comes before interest, he writes, and the lender gains without doing any business. David Hoeschel printed it at Augsburg in 1595.

traces: At the Council of Trent in 1562, Sforza Pallavicino writes, the archbishop of Granada cited his first book on the Mass for the view that Christ gave the apostles the power of priesthood at Pentecost.
Gass writes that Mark of Ephesus drew heavily on him and copied him.
His encomium of St Theodora of Thessalonica was printed in the Acta Sanctorum for 5 April, with Papebroch's commentary.
remembered: The notice from Fabricius calls him a thoroughly learned man.
Symeon of Thessalonica calls him the blessed Cabasilas, Nicholas by name, who won the good victory by piety and purity of life.
Gentian Hervet, while he disputed one point, wrote that nothing more devout or more Christian could be said than the rest of the book.
Fabricius's notice says Casaubon read the seven books of The Life in Christ with great pleasure.

uncertain: Whether he became archbishop of Thessalonica. Fabricius says he succeeded his uncle Nilus in that office, and Migne heads him as metropolitan of Thessalonica. Kantakouzenos calls him still a layman in 1353. Gass thinks he took the see some years later and finds him named archbishop no earlier than 1354. Symeon of Thessalonica gives him no see.

How he was Nilus's nephew. Fabricius makes him the son of Nilus's brother. Gass, after George Phrantzes, makes him the son of Nilus's sister. Phrantzes names Nicholas's mother as the sister of an archbishop of Thessalonica, without naming him.

Whether Kabasilas of the sakellion, a church office, is Nicholas. Kantakouzenos names a church official of that title as an envoy in 1343 and 1347, without a first name. Fabricius, Pontanus and Gass take him for Nicholas. In 1353 Kantakouzenos counts that Kabasilas among the leading clergy, a few pages before he calls Nicholas a layman.
Whether Nikephoros Gregoras's old friend Cabasilas is Nicholas. Gregoras names only a Cabasilas, in deep old age in 1351. His editor Boivin and Gass take him for Nicholas.

Which writings against the Latins are his. Fabricius says not all agree that he wrote against them or against Thomas Aquinas. Gass gives those titles to Nilus. Louis Petit gives a tract on purgatory to Barlaam of Calabria.
